l: Corybantes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Corybantes, goddesses identified with Curetes, were placed on Samothracia by mother of gods; in Sicily, Cretans built a temple, and Delphi's oracle directed cities to honor them.

l: genealogy of the gods, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The reported genealogy begins with Uranus and Titea, whose children include the Titans, Basilea, and Rhea. It further traces the divine status of Helios, Selene, and Cybele.

l: Uranus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Uranus is the first king of the Atlantides, ruling much of the world, especially westward and northward. He settles wandering people in towns and cities, teaches useful practices and the use and storage of earth’s fruits, and measures time by the sun and moon. After death, his prognostications and astronomical skill lead to his honor as a god.

l: Terra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Titea, mother of Uranus’s eighteen children collectively called Titans, is remembered after death as the goddess Terra because of her wisdom and beneficence.

l: Basilea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Basilea, Uranus and Titea’s eldest and most prudent daughter, raised her brothers with maternal care and became the Great Mother. After her father’s death, the people and her brothers elected her queen while she was still a virgin; though initially unwilling, she married Hyperion to leave heirs.

l: Hyperion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Hyperion, Basilea’s brother and beloved husband, fathered Helios and Selene. Said to have discovered the motions of the sun, moon, and stars, seasons, and divisions of time, he taught their nature and was called father of the planets. Envious brothers assassinated him.

l: Cybele, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cybele is a goddess, called the Mother of the Mountains and worshiped as the mother of the gods. Said to originate in Phrygia, she was abandoned on Mount Cybelus and nursed by leopards and other wild beasts. She invented the multi-reed pipe, timbrel, and cymbal, and learned to treat diseases in children and cattle. She married Jasion, bore Corybas, traveled to Phrygia with Dardanus and Corybas, and brought sacred mysteries into Asia. After Atys and her nurses died, she wandered madly before Phrygians worshiped her.

l: Marsyas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A Phrygian, ingenious and chaste, associated with Cybele, invented the hautboy, followed Cybele in madness, challenged Apollo in music, was defeated, and flayed alive.

l: Atys (Papas), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Atys, later called Papas, was a young native whom Cybele loved and accompanied, becoming pregnant by him. Cybele's father ordered Atys and her nurses to be killed after learning of the pregnancy, and the bodies were left without burial.

l: Phrygians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Phrygians, afflicted by plague and famine, sought an oracle, were told to bury Atys and worship Cybele, made a statue when Atys’s body was missing, held funeral rites and yearly sacrifices, and built Cybele’s temple at Pessinunte with King Midas’s aid.

l: Atlas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Atlas receives by lot the country bordering the ocean, calls its people after himself, and is counted among the most renowned children of Coelus after Hyperion's death. An excellent astrologer and first discoverer of knowledge of the sphere, he studies astrology and possesses a wrought sphere of stars; these give rise to the belief that he carries the world on his shoulders. The greatest mountain bears his name. He has many sons, including Hesperus, and seven daughters, the Atlantides; another record calls Hesperus his brother and names Hesperis as his wife and the mother of the Atlantides and Hesperides. After Hercules returns abducted girls, Atlas assists him and teaches him astrology.

l: contest between Marsyas and Apollo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Marsyas and Apollo competed to determine who was the greater artist, with the Nysians serving as judges. Apollo ultimately won after performing with his harp and voice, and Marsyas was subsequently flayed alive.

l: worship of Cybele, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The worship of Cybele began after the people believed Basilea, or the mother described in the account, was a goddess. The Phrygians later instituted sacrifices and divine rites for Cybele, built her a magnificent temple at Pessinunte with the assistance of King Midas, and placed leopards and lions beside her statue.

l: Atlantides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a daughters of Atlas [collective name] The Atlantides were Atlas’s seven daughters: Maia, Electra, Taygeta, Asterope, Merope, Halcyone, and Celseno. They bore sons by heroic princes and gods, becoming ancestors of nations and cities; after their deaths they were worshipped as goddesses and placed among the stars as the Pleiades. Nymphs were also commonly called Atlantides because nympha was a general term for women in that country.

l: Curetes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Curetes were goddesses associated with Crete and Sicily, honored by Cretans in Sicily and neighboring peoples. Nine mountain- and cave-dwelling Curetes managed flocks, developed food-gathering and warfare practices, organized communities, and invented armed dancing. Their noisy dance helped conceal and raise Jupiter, protecting him from Saturn.

l: Ida, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ida was the Cretan mountain associated with the Idæi Dactyli and the upbringing of Jupiter. Its cave was said to have concealed Jupiter, and the surrounding places were consecrated to him.

l: vine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Vine is a plant naturally produced by earth. It shoots branches and bears grapes, including wild grapes without cultivation; its growth, fruiting, destruction, pruning, and renewed flourishing were represented through Bacchus’s births, dismemberment, boiling, and revival.

l: Proserpina, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_associated_with Sicily [as a deity to whom the island is dedicated] Proserpina was the daughter of Ceres and was carried off by Pluto. Her abduction caused Ceres to grieve and burn the corn, and her recovery led Ceres to reconcile with Jupiter and distribute seed-corn through Triptolemus.

l: Naxians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Naxians, first to defect from Xerxes, credited Bacchus, raised among them and favoring their island, with aid against barbarians and their wealth, power, fleet, victories, and wine.

l: Nysa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Nysa is an island city surrounded by Triton, entered only through the Nysian gates. Fertile, beautiful, and healthful with meadows, gardens, streams, caves, flowers, trees, and birds, it is where Bacchus was raised and instructed.

l: Pelasgi, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Pelasgi were described as a nation accustomed to arms and wandering from their ancient habitations. They settled part of Crete after the Eteocretans and were also the first people said to seize and inhabit deserted Lesbos.

l: Laomedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Laomedon is king of Troy and father of Priam. He refuses promised horses, imprisons Iphiclus and Telamon, and plots against the Argonauts after withholding Hesione. Hercules attacks Troy, kills Laomedon and many Trojans, and takes the city.

l: Amalthaea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Amalthaea is a beautiful virgin encountered by Ammon in the Ceraunean mountains. She bears his son, Bacchus, becomes queen of the fertile Western Horn, and sees her child sent to Nysa because Ammon fears Rhea’s jealousy.

l: Aristaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Aristaeus, son of Apollo and Cyrene, was raised by nymphs, who named him Agreus and taught him cheese-making, beekeeping, and olive cultivation. Prudent, honest, and learned, he tutored Bacchus, first sacrificed to him as a god, married Autonoe, and fathered Actaeon. He aided Coos, Sardinia, and Sicily, learned Bacchus’s rites in Thrace, disappeared near Mount Hiemus, and was worshipped as a god for useful arts.

l: the Argonaut expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Argonaut expedition, led by Jason and joined by Hercules, sails from Iolchos to Colchis for the Golden Fleece. Its participants endure storms, hostile peoples, battles, and other dangers, obtain the fleece, defeat the Colchians, and begin their return.

l: Europa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_the_daughter_of Agenor [and is reported to have been carried to Crete on a bull] Europa was the daughter of Agenor and the mother, by Jupiter, of Minos and Rhadamanthus. She was reportedly carried into Crete on the back of a bull through the providence of the gods.

l: Mnemosyne, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: invents letters and writing [through logic and naming] Mnemosyne was said to have discovered logic and assigned proper names to things so that discourse could be clearly understood. She was also credited with whatever assisted human memory.

l: Gerion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: has Gerion's grove [a grove consecrated to him as a demi-god] Gerion was one of the sons of Chrysaor and was associated with the remarkable herds of cattle taken by Hercules. Hercules later consecrated a grove to Gerion as to a demi-god, and the inhabitants worshipped him.

l: centaurs, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Centaurs are hybrid beings, horse-like in body and human in understanding, with reported origins from Ixion and Nephele or a cloud shaped like Juno. They fight the Lapiths, attack women at Perithous and Hippodamia’s marriage feast, raid neighbors, then attack Hercules after Pholus opens wine; Hercules kills many and drives the rest away.

l: India expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dionysius’s India expedition lasts three years, then ends in Boeotia with his return carrying spoils and an Indian elephant, commemorated by recurring festivals.

l: twelve labours of Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The twelve labours of Hercules are tasks imposed by Eurystheus after an oracle at Delphi says Hercules must perform them for immortality. They are extraordinarily numerous and difficult, including killing the Nemean lion and Hydra of Lerna; capturing the Erymanthian boar and golden-horned hind; driving away the Stymphalian birds; cleansing Augeas's stable; bringing the Cretan bull; obtaining Diomedes's mares and Hippolyta's belt; and bringing Cerberus out of hell. After his tenth labour, Eurystheus imposes another: the last is fetching the golden apples of the Hesperides. On completion, Hercules expects immortality.

l: antiquities of the Grecians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The antiquities of the Grecians are the subject of this book. They include accounts of gods, demi-gods, famous warriors, inventors of beneficial practices, and law-makers from the most ancient times.

l: wine-making, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dionysius is credited with discovering the use of wine and teaching people how to plant the vine. He also taught the making of a barley drink called Zythus in countries where vines could not be grown.

l: Creon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: dies_in burning of the Corinthian palace Creon, king of Corinth, agreed to Jason’s marriage to Glauce and ordered Medea to leave the city with one day to prepare. He was consumed by the fire that Medea set in the palace.

l: Iolaus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Iolaus is Hercules’s nephew, associate, captain, and companion in expeditions. After Hercules’s tenth labour, he led the Thespiadae colony to Sardinia, defeated its inhabitants, took possession of the island, founded cities, divided fertile land among settlers, and established public schools, temples, and other monuments. The people were named Iolaeians after him, and colonists in Sardinia and Sicily honored him as a father and demi-god. After Hercules’s translation to the gods, Iolaus helped command Heraclid forces with Theseus and Hyllus against Eurystheus, then went with the Heraclidae and allies from Trachina, later returning toward Greece and Sicily.

l: Nemean lion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a monster [of monstrous size and invulnerable to weapons] The Nemean lion is a monstrous beast whose hide cannot be pierced or wounded by weapons or stones. Hercules traps it in its den, strangles it with his arms, and thereafter wears its skin as protection.

l: Hydra of Lerna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a monster [with a hundred necks and regenerative heads] The Hydra of Lerna has a hundred necks and serpent heads, with two heads growing whenever one is cut off. Hercules has Iolaus burn the severed parts to stop them from regenerating, kills the monster, and dips his arrows in its gall so that their wounds cannot be healed.

l: Daphnis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Daphnis, Mercury’s son by a nymph, is raised by nymphs in Sicily’s Berei Mountains and becomes a herd-owning shepherd, hunter with Diana, composer, and inventor of bucolic songs. After lying with a king’s daughter despite warning, he becomes blind.

l: Pasiphae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Minos’s wife becomes enamored of a bull after his failed sacrifice, uses an artificial cow with Daedalus’s help, and bears the Minotaur.

l: Jason, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Jason, son of Aeson and nephew of Pelias, is an ambitious heroic adventurer and captain of the Argonaut expedition. Seeking fame, he leads the Argonauts to Colchis, promises marriage to Medea for her aid, helps seize the Golden Fleece, and is wounded during the escape before Medea cures him. Though Thessaly believes the Argonauts lost, Pelias destroys Jason’s family. Jason returns, attacks Pelias’s palace with the Argonauts, and places Acastus on the throne. After dedicating Argo to Neptune, he settles in Corinth with Medea, abandons her for Glauce, and, after Medea destroys the palace and kills their children, dies by suicide in misery.

l: Colchis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Colchis is a kingdom ruled by Aeetes, containing Mars's temple and Golden Fleece; Jason and Argonauts arrive with Medea, take it, defeat pursuing Colchians, and depart.

l: golden fleece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Golden Fleece is the skin of the ram on which Phryxus traveled to Colchis, said in one account to be gilded with gold. It hangs in the temple of Mars, guarded by Colchian forces and, according to poets, a dragon. Jason and the Argonauts seize and carry it away with Medea's help.

l: Antiope, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Antiope, queen of the Amazons, is captured by Theseus, taken to battle against the Amazons, defends him bravely, and dies there.

l: the tenth labour of Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The tenth labour imposed upon Hercules was to drive away Gerion’s oxen from Iberia; he defeated Chrysaor’s three sons, took the herds, and completed it.

l: oxen of Gerion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Gerion’s oxen pastured near the ocean in Iberia; Hercules drove them away, transported them through his expedition, then brought them to Sicily and Italy.

l: Iberia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Iberia is a broad, fertile, mineral-rich country of several peoples, with silver, gold, brass, and tin and mountains that sheltered raiders. Ruled by Chrysaor and defended by his sons’ armies, it was gained by Hercules after he defeated them and drove away Gerion’s oxen; he later entrusted its government to leading inhabitants.

l: sons of Chrysaor, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Three strong-bodied, martial sons of Chrysaor each command a large army; during a tenth labour, Hercules challenges and slays their three generals in single combat, gaining Iberia and herds of oxen.

l: Pillars of Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Hercules erected the Pillars of Hercules on opposite sides of the strait near the ocean, as lasting monuments of his expedition. The text also reports competing accounts that he either narrowed the passage by building up the mountains or cut a trench through joined continents.

l: Ligurians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ligurians are a group inhabiting Liguria, a rough, barren, mountainous, wooded land difficult to cultivate. Constant labour and scarce crops shape their hunting, gathering, tree-cutting, and rock-breaking. Men and women live in fields, hollow rocks, or caves; lean, strong, daring, lightly armed people also sail small vessels through dangerous seas.

l: Tiber, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_the_site_of Rome [Rome stands there in the author's time] The Roman army crossed the Tiber before meeting the Gauls. After the defeat at the Allia, many Romans tried to escape by swimming across it, and Pontius Camillus later crossed it by night to reach the Capitol.

l: Proserpine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Proserpine is a goddess said to have lived with Ceres and Diana in Enna before Pluto carried her away. Connected with Sicilian festivals, spring, and Lake Cyane, she is moved by Orpheus’s music and permits his wife’s return, then kindly allows Hercules to free Theseus and Pirithous.

l: Rhegium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Rhegium was first the name of the place where the narrow neck connecting Sicily to the continent was said to have been severed; many years later a city was built there. A key of Italy, it supported Syracusan exiles and repeatedly opposed Dionysius, rejecting his marriage proposal, receiving his enemies, resisting an attack, and aiding against his fleet. After a truce, Dionysius imposed tribute, hostages, and the surrender of seventy ships, then besieged the city. Rhegium endured eleven months of siege and extreme famine before surrendering; many citizens were imprisoned, sold as slaves, or punished.

l: Locris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: has_inhabitants the inhabitants of Locris Locris was the place where Zaleuchus was born. Its people chose him to make their laws.

l: Eryx, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_son_of Venus Eryx was said to be the son of Venus and a famous Sicilian prince. He became king of part of Sicily, founded the city called Eryx on a high hill, and built a temple to Venus there.

l: Butes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Butes, Boreas’s younger son, plots to murder his brother and is exiled with accomplices; leading Thracians to Strongyle, he pirates and ravishes Coronides, is maddened by Bacchus, and dies by casting himself into a pit.

l: Leontines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Leontines is a Sicilian colony of Chalcidican and original Athenian descent. Driven out and oppressed by the Syracusans, it appealed to Athens, whose league Gorgias helped secure. During the Athenian expedition, however, Leontines made peace with Syracuse, and the Athenian fleet returned home.

l: Peloponnesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Peloponnesus is a place containing Pylos, largely subdued by Pelops after he gained the kingdom of Pisa and named after him. After the translation of Hercales to the gods, the Heraclidae invaded under Hyllus; after his death they delayed their return for fifty years, then returned. It later received people withdrawing from Athens, Boeotia, and other threatened regions, who treated it as a refuge and defense and fortified its isthmus. Its central history is conflict: allied with the Lacedaemonians, it sent forces from its borders to invade Attica, while Athenians repeatedly raided its coasts, burned towns, destroyed castles, plundered, invaded, and ravaged it. Fortified Pylos made it a major theater of war, though a five-year peace followed. Finally, cities conspired against the Lacedaemonians, put war direction in Argos, and the region fractured through shifting alliances, fighting between Argos and Sparta, and political upheaval.

l: Tempe, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Tempe was selected as a passage to be defended against the Persians. The Greek forces abandoned it after learning that most Thessalians and the inhabitants of the nearby straits had submitted to the king.

l: Thessaly, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: contains Diros [mountain] The Greeks sent ten thousand armed men into Thessaly to occupy the passages at Tempe. Much of Thessaly later submitted to the Persian commissioners, causing the Greek forces to withdraw.

l: Dorieus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dorieus, Peloponnesian admiral of Italian galleys, left Rhodes for Hellespont, defended ships at Dardanium after Athenian surprise until Mindarus arrived.

l: Argonauts, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Argonauts are a group of heroes and distinguished companions chosen by Jason, numbered as three-and-forty men in one record and fifty-four eager volunteers in another, including Hercules, Castor, Pollux, Telamon, Orpheus, and Atalanta. Sailing on Argo, they travel to Colchis, take the Golden Fleece from the temple of Mars at night, fight the Colchians, and suffer wounded before Medea helps them sail home. They also land at Byzantium, pass through the Propontis, Hellespont, Troy, and Samothracia, rescue Iphiclus and Telamon, dedicate offerings, prepare to aid Jason against Pelias, and dedicate Argo to Neptune.

l: Theseus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Theseus, son of Aethra, is a brave ruler whose deeds shape his rise and fall. On his journey to Athens, he kills several foes and masters the Marathonian bull. Recognized by Aegeus, he kills the Minotaur with Ariadne’s help, escapes the labyrinth, carries Ariadne away, and comes from Crete with her; after a threatening dream, he abandons her on an island. He carries away Antiope or Hippolyte, incurs Amazonian hatred, and defeats the Amazons in Attica. As Aegeus’s successor and king of Athens, he gathers the country’s scattered people into Athens, marries Phaedra, and has sons. After attempting to court Proserpina, he is imprisoned in the underworld. Sedition drives him into exile, where he dies; Athens later returns his bones, honors him as a god, and establishes the Theseum sanctuary.

l: golden apples of the Hesperides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The golden apples of the Hesperides, object of Hercules's last labour after his tenth, were regarded either as actual golden apples guarded by a dragon or poetically as sheep.

l: Hesperides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: are_daughters_of Atlas [also called Atlantides after their father] The Hesperides were associated with a garden or country called Hesperis and were said by some mythologists to possess golden apples guarded by a dragon. Other accounts interpreted the golden apples as sheep or as their golden-colored fleeces.

l: sheep of the Hesperides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The sheep of the Hesperides were described by some writers as animals of exquisite beauty. They were poetically called golden apples, either because of their appearance or because their fleeces glittered like gold.

l: Hippolytus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Hippolytus was Theseus’s son by the Amazon and was sent to Troezene to be raised by Aethra. When Phaedra solicited him and he refused her, she falsely accused him of attempting to ravish her. While driving a chariot, Hippolytus was so disturbed by the accusation that he dropped the reins; the horses dragged him to his death. The Troezenians later adored him as a god because of his commendable chastity.

l: battle of Theseus and the Amazons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_won_by Theseus [through the valour of the Athenians] In the battle in Attica, Theseus led an army raised from the citizens against the Amazons. The Athenians won, killed some of the Amazons, and drove the rest from Attica; Antiope died while defending Theseus.

l: Sardinia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sardinia is an island as large as Sicily, fertile and cultivated. Hercules, following an oracle, established a colony there governed by the sons of the Thespiadae under Iolaus. Later the Carthaginians conquered it, but its lolaeian inhabitants withdrew to mountains and resisted both Carthaginian and Roman subjugation.

l: Thespiadae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: are_sons_of Hercules [fifty sons born to the fifty daughters of Thespis] The Thespiadae were the fifty sons born to Hercules by the fifty daughters of Thespis. Most were sent with Iolaus to establish a colony in Sardinia, while two remained in Thebes and seven settled in the city of Thespis.

l: colony of the Thespiadae in Sardinia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The colony of the Thespiadae in Sardinia, established under Iolaus, defeated inhabitants and gained fertile Iolaion; it prospered through cultivation, mixed with barbarians, and eventually lived in inaccessible mountains.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Carthaginians are a people and African power, centered in Africa and operating through armies, fleets, confederates, mercenaries, colonies, mines, and overseas possessions. They seek wealthy and strategic islands, coveting Sardinia, settling Pityusa, conquering Sardinia, opposing an Etrurian colonization plan, and controlling Spain. By opening and exploiting Iberian silver mines, they gain wealth sufficient to hire many soldiers and wage extensive wars. Their principal unfolding conflict is in Sicily. An early invasion under Amilcar ends in rout at Himera, followed by peace payments and promises. Later, desiring to protect Egesta, they assemble forces from Africa and Campania, invade again, take Selinus, defeat and destroy Himera, and return with prisoners and plunder. They build Therma, recruit widely, and undertake larger campaigns: besieging, starving, plundering, and occupying Agrigentum; preparing weapons and engines; attacking Gela; and devastating territory around Gela and Camarina. Plague repeatedly weakens their armies and helps bring peace or military reverses. They defend Motya but lose it, then raise another large army and fleet from Africa, Spain, confederates, and mercenaries, capture Motya and Messana, defeat a Sicilian fleet, and besiege Syracuse. Disease and Syracusan attacks destroy their camp, forts, fleet, and transports. Routed by sea and land, they lose their Sicilian possessions and face revolt among African confederates. Confined to Carthage, they seek religious appeasement through sacrifices to Proserpina and Ceres, then defeat the rebels with officers, Sardinian supplies, and rebel divisions. Under Mago they attempt recovery, suffer defeat near Abacene, renew war with a large landing force, and finally make peace after shortages and attacks on provisions.

l: Omphale, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Omphale, daughter of Jardanus and queen of the Maeonians, receives Hercules as a slave, recognizes and frees him, marries him, and becomes mother of their son Lamon.

l: Troas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_ruled_by Teucer [first ruler of the country] Troas was the country ruled first by Teucer and later associated with the descendants of Tros. Ilus founded Ilium in its plain.

l: Amphiaraus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Amphiaraus, a soothsayer married to Eriphyle, foresaw death in the war against Thebes. Despite this, Eriphyle’s judgment and gifts led him to go; earth swallowed him and his chariot, after he ordered Alcmaeon to kill her.

l: Telamon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Aeacus’s son fled Aegina for Salamis, became king through marriage, then, widowed and remarried, fathered Ajax.

l: Augeas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_king_of Eleans Augeas defrauded Hercules of his promised reward. Hercules later invaded Elis, killed Augeas, took the city, and restored Phyleus to the kingdom because Phyleus had judged that the reward should be given to Hercules.

l: Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sparta is a Greek power, militarily active in Greece and Asia, lying close to the sides of Peloponnesus and described as a castle or bulwark defending it. After Hercules defeated Hippocoon and his sons and took Sparta, he restored Tyndarus to its kingdom on condition that he preserve it for his posterity. Sparta sent Leonidas to command Thermopylae, where the expedition was presented as dying for common liberty and advancing Sparta’s fame. It detained Themistocles and other ambassadors during an inspection of Athens’s walls, then released them; it ordered Pausanias to free Greek cities from Persian garrisons but later punished him for treason. Pausanias’s conduct brought contempt, though Hetaemaridas prevented war with Athens for dominion of the sea. A devastating earthquake killed more than twenty thousand people, after which Helots and Messenians attacked. Sparta supported Megara against Athens despite being poorer and weaker at sea, recovered after losses at Sphacteria, defeated Argives and allies at Mantinea, received Alcibiades, opposed Persian power in Asia, and imposed terms on Elis and Messenia. Its tyrannical government caused hatred among confederates.

l: Hyllus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Hyllus, son of Hercules, helps command Heraclid forces, kills Eurystheus during his flight, then dies in single combat against Echemus.

l: Auge, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Auge was the daughter of Aleus and secretly became pregnant by Hercules. Aleus ordered that she be drowned, but she was spared, sold to Teuthras, and eventually found her son Telephus.

l: Telephus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Telephus was the son of Hercules and Auge. After Auge left him hidden on Mount Parthenius, shepherds found him being suckled by a hind and brought him to Corythus, who raised him. He later discovered his mother through an oracle, married Teuthras's daughter Agriopa, and became Teuthras's heir and successor.

l: Deianira, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Deianira was the daughter of Oeneus. After Meleager had died, Hercules married her when he came to Calydon.

l: Oeneus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Oeneus, king of Calydonia and father of Meleager, neglected Diana in sacrifice after abundant corn, then married Periboea and had Tydeus.

l: Meleager, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Meleager, son of Oeneus, joins the hunt for the Calydonian boar, first wounds it, and gives its skin to Atalanta, whom he loves. He defends her against the sons of Thestius and kills them when they refuse to return the skin. He later dies before Hercules comes to Calydon.

l: oracle of Apollo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The oracle warned Laius that having a son would bring disaster because the son would kill him. It later directed Adrastus's marriages, promised victory to the Epigoni if Alcmaeon led them, and commanded Alcmaeon both to undertake the war and avenge Amphiaraus by killing Eriphyle.

l: sacred Samothracian mysteries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: are_observed_in Samothracia [ancient rites and ceremonies] The sacred Samothracian mysteries were ancient rites observed on Samothracia and newly revived in the account. They could not ordinarily be heard by the uninitiated, but Jupiter was said to have revealed them to Jasion and to have initiated strangers.

l: Hercules's marriage to Deianira, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Hercules's marriage to Deianira took place at Calydon after Meleager's death. Deianira was the daughter of Oeneus.

l: Calydonian boar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A mighty, famous beast sent by Diana as punishment after Oeneus failed to sacrifice to her, it ravages Calydonia and cattle until Meleager and other hunters pursue it.

l: Calydonian boar hunt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Calydonian boar hunt was undertaken by Meleager and many other notable hunters. Meleager first wounded the boar, and the hunters generally agreed that he should receive the boar's skin and the honor of the deed.

l: Atalanta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Atalanta, Eclieneus's daughter and a hunter among Meleager's associates, joins the Calydonian boar hunt, receives its skin and glory from Meleager, then loses it to Thestius's sons.

l: Althea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: curses Meleager [after her brothers' deaths] Althea was Meleager's mother and the sister of the men he killed. She grieved excessively over their deaths, cursed Meleager, and wished the gods would destroy him; after his death she regretted her action and hanged herself.

l: Meleager's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_caused_by Althea [according to the account in which her curse is heard] Meleager was killed after Althea cursed him, and the gods heard her prayer. Another account says that his life depended on a firebrand preserved by Althea, which she threw into the fire after her brothers' deaths, thereby hastening his death.

l: Achelous, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_identified_with river Achelous [in the explanatory account of the myth] Achelous was diverted by Hercules into a channel that he cut, watering much of the Calydonian country and making it exceedingly fruitful. The account connects this work with the poetic story of Hercules fighting Achelous in the form of a bull and cutting off one of his horns.

l: Dejanira, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dejanira was Hercules's wife. After learning of his love for Iole, she anointed his coat and shirt with the substance supplied by Nessus; when Hercules was dying from it, she recognized what she had done and hanged herself.

l: Nessus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Nessus is a centaur and hired ferryman at the Evenus who, after carrying Dejanira across, attempts to ravish her. Hercules shoots him; dying, Nessus gives Dejanira instructions for a substance meant to compel Hercules’s love.

l: Nessus's love potion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a love potion [made from Nessus's blood and seed] Nessus told Dejanira to mix his blood, oil, and some of his seed and use the mixture on Hercules's undergarment. Dejanira later applied the substance to Hercules's coat and shirt, believing it would preserve his love for her, but it acted as a destructive poison.

l: Dorians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dorians settle Crete under Teutamus, enroll in Himera, then lose and regain Parnassus cities with Lacedaemonian aid.

l: Lapithae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Lapiths took their name from Lapithus, who ruled near the river Peneus. Their later conflict with the Centaurs led to many deaths and forced survivors to flee to Pholoe and Malea.

l: Iole, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Iole was the daughter of Eurytus. After Hercules defeated the sons of Eurytus for refusing to give her to him in marriage, he carried Iole away to the promontory of Cenaeum.

l: Hercules's poisoned garment, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: causes Hercules's death [through its venomous poison] Dejanira anointed Hercules's coat and shirt with the substance given by Nessus, and Lichas carried them to Hercules. When Hercules put them on, the poison spread through the garment, scorched his body, and caused intolerable torment.

l: Hercules's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_caused_by Hercules's poisoned garment [after the poison causes intolerable torment] After the poisoned garment caused his suffering, Hercules returned to Trachinia and sought an oracle's advice. He was carried to Mount Oeta, placed upon a funeral pile, and burned after Philoctetes set it alight; no bones were found, leading to the belief that he had been translated from humanity to the gods.

l: Medea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Medea, daughter of Aeetes and Hecate and sister of Circe, uses powerful poisons, herbs, roots, and stratagems. Opposing Aeetes’s murder of strangers, she escapes imprisonment, aids Jason and the Argonauts in Colchis, poisons the dragon guarding the Golden Fleece, and treats their wounded. She later helps bring down Pelias, lives with Jason in Corinth, burns the palace after his marriage to Glauce, kills most of their children, flees to Hercules, marries Aegeus in Athens, and later goes to Asia in some accounts.

l: Pelias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Pelias is a king of Thessaly, Jason’s homeland, who rules Iolchus and neighboring countries and is Jason’s uncle. Son of Tyro and Neptune, and later called son of Cretheus, he fears Æson and Jason as threats to his kingdom. He sends Jason on the dangerous voyage to Colchis hoping he will die, then, believing Jason and the other heroes have perished, destroys Jason’s family by forcing Jason’s father to drink bull’s blood and murdering the child Promachus. He also conflicts with Neleus and enters the Peloponnese with Melampus and Bias. Medea deceives him with a promise of restored youth, leading Pelias’s daughters, except Alcestis, to kill him.

l: Argo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Argo is an unusually large ship built at Pelion for Jason’s expedition, named either after Argus, who repairs it, or for swift sailing. Dedicated to Neptune, it carries Jason and the Argonauts to Colchis and back, then is dedicated at the Isthmus of Peloponnesus.

l: Mount Athos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: has Athos canal [a cut through the mountain] Xerxes sent another body of men to cut a passage through Mount Athos. The work was completed quickly and was intended to shorten and secure the army's route.

l: Dardanus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dardanus, son of Jupiter and Electra and husband of Batia, left Samothracia for Asia, founded Dardanum, established Troy, succeeded Teucer as king, and gave his name to the Dardanians.

l: Medea's rescue of the Argonauts, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_performed_by Medea [through compassion and magical skill] Medea rescues and assists the Argonauts by informing them of the danger from the local custom of murdering strangers and guiding them to the temple of Mars. She helps them enter, poisons the ever-watchful dragon guarding the fleece, and later cures Jason, Laertes, Atalanta, and the Thespiades of wounds received in battle.

l: capture of the Golden Fleece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_performed_by Argonauts [with Medea's assistance] Medea leads the Argonauts at night to the temple of Mars, where guards admit her because she is the king's daughter. The Argonauts kill many defenders, drive the rest away, take down the Golden Fleece, and hurry back to their ship while Medea poisons the dragon that guards it.

l: Byzantium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Byzantium, named after Byzas, held a strong Peloponnesian garrison, was besieged and jointly attacked by Theramenes and Alcibiades, and was entered through betrayal by some Byzantines. It was restored to the Byzantines and renewed its alliance with Athenians. Later, amid sedition and war with Thracians, Clearchus ruled tyrannically until Lacedaemonians attacked him.

l: the taking of Troy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The taking of Troy is attributed by some ancient poets to Hercules. After a battle between the Argonauts and the Trojans, Hercules suddenly assaults Troy, kills Laomedon, punishes the king's supporters, and installs Priam; another account has him take it with six ships without Argonauts.

l: Amphinome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Amphinome, Pelias’s daughter, Andrtemon’s wife, and Promachus’s mother, is sought for slaughter; she runs to the king’s palace, curses Pelias for impiety, then stabs herself to death.

l: Jason's whole family, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_extinguished_by Pelias Pelias extinguished Jason’s whole family before Jason returned to Thessaly. Their destruction led Jason and the Argonauts to prepare an attack against Pelias.

l: Medea's stratagem against Pelias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_devised_by Medea Medea’s stratagem involved entering the city disguised as an aged priestess, presenting a hollow image of Diana, and claiming that the goddess could restore Pelias’s youth. She demonstrated the alleged power by making herself appear young and by producing a lamb from a boiled ram, then delayed the daughters while the Argonauts attacked.

l: Medea's poisons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Medea possessed many powerful poisons, attributed to Hecate or Circe, concealed kinds in Diana’s hollow image, and used enchanted substances in demonstrations.

l: hollow image of Diana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Medea prepares a hollow image of Diana, hides poisons inside it, and carries it into the city to encourage superstitious reverence.

l: Pelias's daughters, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Pelias’s daughters, deceived by Medea, killed Pelias while seeking to restore his youth, then lamented when Jason and the Argonauts entered and were spared.

l: Pelias's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_caused_by Medea [through the deception of Pelias's daughters] Pelias’s daughters, except Alcestis, cudgelled him to death after Medea convinced them that his body had to be boiled to restore his youth. Medea delayed them with prayers to the moon while the Argonauts made their assault.

l: Admetus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Thessalian son of Pheretes and king of the Molossians, Admetus courteously shelters, funds, and secretly helps Themistocles escape Lacedaemonian pressure.

l: Corinth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Corinth is a city marked by refuge, war, and political upheaval. Jason and Medea lived there for ten years; after Medea fled, Corinthians buried her murdered children in Juno’s temple and worshipped them as demi-gods. Corinth received Deucetius in lifelong exile, aided Epidamnus against Corcyra, rebuilt its fleet after defeat, and supported Potidea. It hosted an assembly against the Lacedaemonians, then became the center of the Corinthian War, where sedition, killings, banishments, and fighting ended in Argive control.

l: Glauce, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Glauce, Creon’s daughter, is courted and married by Jason after he abandons Medea, then dies with Creon in the burning Corinthian palace; another account attributes her death to poisoned plasters.

l: Medea and Jason's marriage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: lasts ten years [in Corinth] Medea and Jason lived as husband and wife in Corinth for ten years and had three children. Their marriage ended when Jason married Glauce.

l: Jason's abandonment of Medea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: results_in Medea [being commanded to leave Corinth] Jason sought a divorce from Medea and then married Glauce, explaining that he wanted heirs to the royal family. Medea appealed to the gods who had witnessed his vows, but Jason proceeded without further regard for her.

l: burning of the Corinthian palace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_caused_by Medea [by witchcraft] After being ordered to leave Corinth, Medea entered the palace at night and used a root associated with Circe that could not be extinguished once kindled. The palace burned, Jason escaped, and Glauce and Creon were consumed.

l: Medea and Jason's children, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Medea and Jason's children were twins Thessalus and Alcimena, then Tisandrus; Medea murdered all but one, and the survivor escaped by flight.

l: murder of Medea's children, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_committed_by Medea [except one child who escapes] Medea murdered her children by cutting their throats, except for one who escaped. She buried them in Juno’s temple, and the Corinthians later followed an oracle’s instruction to worship them as demi-gods.

l: Aegeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Aegeus recognized and accepted Theseus through the tokens that Theseus brought to Athens. He sacrificed the Marathonian bull to Apollo. He sent a pilot with Theseus and ordered that white sails be used if Theseus survived and black sails if he perished. Seeing the returning black sails, Aegeus believed Theseus had died and threw himself from the top of the citadel.

l: the Heraclidae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Heraclidae, children of Hercules, first lived with Ceyx in Trachinia, were expelled at Eurystheus's demand, sheltered by Athenians at Tricorythus and helped defeat him, then after Hyllus's death returned there and settled among Dorians; they held Sparta's kingship until Lysander planned to end it.

l: the kingdom of Mycenae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Eurystheus feared losing the kingdom of Mycenae to the Heraclidae. After Eurystheus's death, Atreus obtained the kingdom.

l: Tricorythus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a city [one of the four cities of Tetrapolis] Tricorythus, one of the four cities of the part of Attica called Tetrapolis, received the Heraclidae and their friends after they fled Trachina. The Heraclidae returned there after Hyllus was killed and remained until the fifty years had expired.

l: the battle between the Heraclids and Eurystheus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Heraclidae, assisted by the Athenians and commanded by Iolaus, Theseus, and Hyllus, fought Eurystheus and routed his army. A great part of Eurystheus's forces was cut off, Eurystheus was killed by Hyllus, and all of Eurystheus's sons fell.

l: the single combat between Hyllus and Echemus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_between Hyllus Hyllus challenged an enemy champion on the condition that victory would give the Heraclidae the kingdom of Eurystheus, while his own death would bar the Heraclidae from Peloponnesus for fifty years. Echemus, king of the Tegeans, accepted the challenge and killed Hyllus.

l: Tlepolemus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Tlepolemus, son of Hercules, fled Argos after killing Licymnius in a quarrel. He went to Rhodes, divided it into three parts, built Lyndus, Jalysus, and Camirus, became king of the Rhodians, and assisted Agamemnon at Troy.

l: Argos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Argos is a place marked by settlement, refuge, and military leadership. Licymnius, his children, and Tlepolemus settled there; Tlepolemus later fled after killing Licymnius. It received Polynices and Tydeus, raised forces against Thebes, then led a coalition, formed a permanent elite thousand, fought Sparta, endured an oligarchic coup, and gained Athenian support.

l: Triopas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Triopas, son of Phorbas, fled after killing his brother, helped expel the Pelasgians in Thessaly, built Triopium in Caria, and gained Chersonesus and adjoining Carian country.

l: Camirus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Camirus, a city built by one of Cercaphus's three sons, was named after its builder; it later received Althasmenes and his followers and contributed inhabitants to Rhodes during incorporation into one city.

l: Rhodians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Rhodians were regarded as Rhodes’s original inhabitants and, after plague swept away earlier inhabitants, settled colonists there. They held Rhodes consecrated to Sol, worshipped him above other gods as their ancestor, and honored Phorbas and Althasmenes as demi-gods. Later they rejected the Lacedaemonian fleet, revolted, received Conon and his navy, and helped seize Egyptian grain ships.

l: Rhadamanthus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Rhadamanthus, son of Jupiter and Europa and brother of Minos, is renowned as the world’s most just man and an inexorable punisher of wickedness. He gains islands and Asian coasts, appoints rulers, and later judges hell with Minos.

l: Androgeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Androgeus, a son of Minos, went to Athens during the Panathenaean solemnities and won all the sports and contests. He became familiar with the sons of Pallas, which made Aegeus jealous. While traveling to Thebes to see a sacred procession, Androgeus was waylaid by country people acting by Aegeus’s order and was murdered near Oenoe in Attica.

l: Ariadne, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ariadne, daughter of Minos, loves and helps Theseus kill the Minotaur and escape the labyrinth. Theseus secretly takes her from Crete but abandons her on Dia. Bacchus takes and marries her, leads her to Mount Arius, and she is not seen again; after her death, her crown becomes a constellation.

l: Asopus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: has_child Aegina [one of twelve daughters] Asopus dwelt at Phlias and married Medon, by whom he had two sons and twelve daughters. His daughters gave their names to places and peoples, including Aegina, Salamis, and Sinope.

l: Phaedra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: accuses Hippolytus [of attempting to ravish her] Phaedra, the daughter of Minos, married Theseus and had Acamantes and Demophon by him. She fell passionately in love with Hippolytus, and when he rejected her, she accused him to Theseus of attempting to ravish her. Fearing that her deception would be discovered, Phaedra hanged herself.

l: Perithous, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Perithous, son of Ixion and Dia, married Hippodamia, invited Theseus and the Centaurs to their wedding, and joined the Lapiths against the drunken Centaurs. After Hippodamia’s death, he went to Athens and joined Theseus in plans to obtain wives. Seeking Proserpina, they descended below and were bound; Theseus was released, but Perithous remained in eternal punishment.

l: Ixion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ixion, Antion’s son, marries Dia but kills her father after withholding a promised dowry; purified by Jupiter, he pursues Juno, fathers Centaurs through a cloud, then is wheel-bound and tortured.

l: Cretans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cretans accompanying Minos to Sicily buried him; after Sicilians burned their ships, they settled there, founded Minoa and Erygum, built a temple, and later received Cretans cast ashore after Troy's destruction.

l: the seven Captains, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The seven captains were Adrastus, Polynices, Tydeus, Amphiaraus, Capaneus, Hippomedon, and Parthenopaeus. They marched against Thebes; all except Adrastus died in the war.

l: the Epigoni, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Epigoni were the children of those slain in the first war against Thebes. Led by Alcmaeon, they defeated the Thebans, entered and razed Thebes, and returned home with spoil.

l: Aegina, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a city [besieged by the Athenians after the Aeginetans were subdued] Aegina was invaded by an Athenian army, which laid waste its countryside and resolved to raze its city. Its defenders later lost a naval battle and submitted to Athens.

l: Lacedaemon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Lacedaemon was asked by Syracuse to provide aid and sent Gylippus, followed by additional troops. At the instigation of Alcibiades, it broke its league with Athens, beginning a renewed war.

l: the Minotaur's tribute, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Athenians were required to send seven boys and seven girls to Minos for seven years so that the Minotaur could devour them. When the seven years had expired, Minos came again and demanded fourteen children, and the Athenians delivered them.

l: the murder of Androgeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The murder of Androgeus was arranged by Aegeus because he feared that Androgeus’s association with the sons of Pallas, aided by Minos, might deprive him of his kingdom. Androgeus was ambushed and killed near Oenoe in Attica. Minos sought justice for the murder, and the resulting conflict led to drought, famine, war, and the Minotaur’s tribute.

l: war against Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The war against Thebes arose after Eteocles refused to surrender the government to Polynices according to their agreement. Adrastus organized the expedition with Polynices, Tydeus, and the other captains, but the army was defeated and nearly all its leaders were killed.

l: Laius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Laius, king of Thebes and husband of Jocasta, consulted an oracle about children, exposed Oedipus after a warning, and was later unknowingly killed by his son on a Phocis road.

l: Jocasta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a daughter [of Creon] Jocasta was the daughter of Creon and the wife of Laius. She later married Oedipus unknowingly and bore him Eteocles, Polynices, Antigone, and Ismene.

l: Oedipus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Oedipus was exposed as an infant after Laius pierced his feet, but he was given to the wife of Polybus. He killed Laius without knowing him to be his father, solved the Sphinx's riddle, became king of Thebes, and married Jocasta without knowing she was his mother.

l: Sphinx, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A double-shaped monster comes to Thebes, poses a riddle and destroys those unable to solve it; after Oedipus solves it, she throws herself from a rock and dies.

l: riddle of the Sphinx, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The riddle asked what creature was two-footed, three-footed, and four-footed. Oedipus answered that it was a human being, who crawls on four limbs as an infant, walks on two feet as an adult, and uses a staff as a third foot in old age.

l: kingdom of Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The kingdom of Thebes was offered as part of the reward for solving the Sphinx's riddle. Oedipus obtained it along with Jocasta, and Eteocles and Polynices later agreed to rule it yearly by turns.

l: Eteocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Eteocles, elder brother of Polynices, first reigned under their agreement, refused to surrender government after his year, then fought Polynices; both brothers killed each other.

l: Polynices, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Polynices demanded the government of Thebes when Eteocles's year ended, but Eteocles refused. He fled to Adrastus at Argos, married Adrastus's daughter, helped arrange the expedition against Thebes, and died fighting Eteocles.

l: Adrastus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Adrastus, king of Argos, received Polynices and Tydeus and married his daughters to them by command of the oracle. He prepared the war against Thebes after Tydeus's ambush and survived the expedition when the other captains perished.

l: Tydeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Tydeus, son of Oeneus, fled Aetolia to Argos after killing his nephews. Adrastus sent him to Eteocles as an envoy; Eteocles's men ambushed him, but Tydeus killed all fifty and returned safely.

l: Capaneus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Capaneus joined Adrastus's expedition against Thebes. He was killed while attempting to scale the walls.

l: Hippomedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Hippomedon joined the seven captains in the war against Thebes. He perished in the war.

l: Parthenopaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Parthenopaeus, son of Atalanta and the daughter of Schoeneus, joined Adrastus's expedition against Thebes. He perished in the war.

l: Eriphyle, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Eriphyle, sister of Adrastus and wife of Amphiaraus, judged in favor of Adrastus and that Amphiaraus should join the war. Polynices gave her a golden chain and Thersandra later gave her a rich garment to influence the war's outcome, and Alcmaeon killed her at his father's command.

l: Alcmaeon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Alcmaeon was chosen by the Epigoni as their commander after the oracle promised victory if he led them. He was instructed to wage the war against Thebes and kill his mother, Eriphyle, and he led the forces that defeated the Thebans.

l: second war against Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The second war against Thebes was undertaken by the Epigoni to avenge their fathers' deaths. The Epigoni defeated the Thebans, who abandoned the city, after which the city was entered and razed.

l: Tiresias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Tiresias advised the defeated Thebans to abandon Thebes as the only means of preserving themselves. He later died at Tilphossus and was buried by the Cadmeans with great funeral pomp, after which he was worshiped as a god.

l: Harmonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Harmonia, a child of Jupiter and Electra, married Cadmus in a marriage celebrated in the presence of the gods. She was the sister of Jasion.

l: Cadmeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Cadmeans followed Tiresias's advice and fled Thebes at night to Tilphossus. They later buried Tiresias, and in time they invaded the Dorians, expelled them, and settled in their country before some returned to Thebes and the rest remained in Doria.

l: Arne, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Arne, daughter of Aeolus, bore Aeolus and Boeotus by Neptune, was sent to Metapontum, then fled after a quarrel with her sons and accompanied them to the Aeolian Islands.

l: Aeolians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a people The Aeolians are described through traditions concerning the descendants of Aeolus. Their history includes the settlement of Aeolus at the Aeolian Islands and the later origins of the Boeotians.

l: Aeolus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Aeolus, son of Hippotas and descended from Deucalion and Helen, arrived at Lipara with companions, married Cyane, and ruled the island. He helped Liparus recover Italian territory, received demi-god honors, and was credited with teaching sailors about sails and predicting winds. A separate Aeolus descended from Mimas is distinguished from him.

l: Aeolian Islands, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Aeolian Islands are seven islands in the Tyrrhenian seas between Sicily and Italy, about one hundred and fifty furlongs from Sicily, marked by visible volcanic openings and eruptions and linked by tradition with Liparus and Aeolus.

l: Lipara, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Lipara is the largest named city and island of the Aeolian group, said to have been founded by Liparus. Its inhabitants shared and cultivated land, resisted Tyrrhenian piracy, and became wealthy through harbors, medicinal baths, fish, fruit, and abundant alum.

l: Salmoneus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Salmoneus, son of Helen and nephew of Aeolus, established himself in Elis and founded Salmone; cruel and impious, he was killed by Zeus with a thunderbolt.

l: Tyro, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Tyro, beautiful daughter of Salmoneus, bore Pelias and Neleus by Neptune, then married Cretheus and had Amythaon, Pheretes, and Aeson.

l: Neleus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Son of Tyro and Neptune, Neleus enters Messenia, founds Pylos, marries Chloris, and fathers twelve sons including Nestor.

l: Pylos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Pylos is a naturally fortified place in Messenia, four hundred stadia from Messene, founded by Neleus after bordering inhabitants gave him territory. Demosthenes walled it in twenty days, and the Athenians defended it against a large Lacedaemonian land and sea force, using it to threaten Laconia and block supplies to Sphacterian island. After fifteen years, its Messenian garrison surrendered under siege, losses, and lack of provisions, and it passed to the Lacedaemonians.

l: Messenia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a country [hostile to Sparta] Sparta prepared for war against Messenia after making peace with its neighbors. The Messenians were expelled from their settlements in Cephallenia and Naupactus and driven from Greece.

l: Nestor, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: commands Trojan War [as one of the Grecian commanders] Nestor was the youngest son of Neleus and Chloris. He went with his brothers to the Trojan War and was one of the Grecian commanders.

l: Lapithus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: rules neighbouring territories [near the Peneus River] Lapithus, descended from Peneus and Stilbes, lived near the river Peneus and ruled the surrounding territory. His sons were Phorbas and Periphas, and the Lapiths took their name from him.

l: Hippodamia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a daughter of Bystus [wife of Perithous] Hippodamia was the daughter of Bystus and the wife of Perithous. Her marriage feast became the occasion for the Centaurs’ attempted assault on the women present.

l: Asclepius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Asclepius, son of Apollo and Coronis, became a famed physician by discovering remedies, surgery, and medicines, and was considered medicine’s first founder; after restoring many apparently dead people, Jupiter killed him with a thunderbolt.

l: Aegina, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Aegina was carried by Jupiter from Phlias to the island that received her name. She bore Aeacus, who later became king of the island.

l: Corcyra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Corcyra, of the same stock as Epidamnus, first refused it aid, then fought the Corinthian-supported settlement, defeated Corinth, and recovered Epidamnus. Later dominant at sea, it sought Athenian support amid violent oligarchic-democratic conflict ending in equal privileges.

l: Aeacus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a son of Zeus and Aegina [later king of Aegina] Aeacus was the son of Jupiter and Aegina and later became king of Aegina. His sons were Peleus and Telamon.

l: Peleus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Peleus, son of Aeacus, accidentally kills Phocus, is banished to Phthia, is purified by Actor, succeeds him as king, and fathers Achilles by Thetis.

l: Ajax, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: commands Trojan War [as an associate in the Trojan war] Ajax was the son of Telamon and Eribna of Athens. He was another associate of Agamemnon in the Trojan War.

l: Pelops, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a son of Tantalus Pelops came to Pisa seeking Hippodamia and bribed Myrtilus to let him win the horse race. He gained Hippodamia and the kingdom of Pisa, then conquered much of the Peloponnese, which was named after him.

l: Tantalus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Tantalus, rich renowned son of Zeus, ruled part of Asia later called Phrygia and fathered Pelops and Niobe; after revealing gods’ secrets to men, he was punished in life and eternally after death.

l: Oenomaus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Oenomaus, son of Mars and Harpina and king of Pisa, fathered Hippodamia; fearing an oracle about her marriage, he killed losing suitors in races until Pelops won, after which he killed himself.

l: Pisa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Pisa was a city of the Peloponnese where Oenomaus ruled. Pelops won Hippodamia there and gained the kingdom.

l: horse race, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a marriage contest [proposed by Oenomaus for Hippodamia's suitors] The horse race ran from Pisa to Neptune’s altar in the isthmus of Corinth. Oenomaus allowed each suitor to start first, then pursued him in a chariot and killed him unless he was overtaken by the suitor.

l: Ilus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Son of Tros, Ilus expels Tantalus from Paphlagonia, then founds Ilium in the plain of Troas.

l: Tros, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Son of Erichthonius and father of Ilus, Assaracus, and Ganymedes, he gives his name to the Trojans.

l: Ilium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ilium was the city founded by Ilus in the plain of Troas.

l: war of the Lapiths and Centaurs, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The war began after the Centaurs, invited to the marriage of Perithous and Hippodamia, became drunk and attempted to ravish the women. Theseus and the Lapiths killed many Centaurs and drove the rest away, after which the Centaurs made war on the Lapiths, killing most of them and forcing the survivors into exile.

l: Talus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Talus, Daedalus's sister's son, trained by Daedalus, surpassed him by inventing useful tools, including potter's wheel and saw, before Daedalus murdered him from jealousy.

l: Icarus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_son_of Daedalus Icarus fled Crete with his father, Daedalus. In one account he fell into the sea while trying to land on an island, and in another he fell when the sun melted the wax holding his artificial wings together; the sea and island were thereafter called Icarian.

l: Cocalus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cocalus, ruler of Sicily, courteously receives and befriends Daedalus, protects him from Minos, then causes Minos’s death in a hot bath and disguises it as an accident.

l: Agrigentum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Agrigentum, also called Minoa after Minos's landing there, was a wealthy Greek city associated with the Agrigentines. Under Theron it conflicted with Syracuse under Thrasideus; after Thrasideus's defeat and death, its people restored democracy and sought peace from Hiero. The Agrigentines later fought the Syracusans after Deucetius was spared without their consent. Long prosperity made Agrigentum comparable in wealth to all Greek cities, with grain and valuables drawn in from its surrounding country, magnificent temples, a vast artificial pond or fishpond, tombs, population, and treasures including the Phalarian bull. Expecting to face the Carthaginian war first, it endured an eight-month Carthaginian siege despite allies. Famine forced evacuation; Amilcar entered, killed remaining people, plundered wealth and art, burned temples, and the Carthaginians occupied it through winter and sacked it again in spring.

l: Venus Erycina, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Venus was called Venus Erycina because of her connection with Eryx and the city he founded. Her worship at Eryx continued under the Sicilians, Carthaginians, and Romans, who greatly enriched her temple.

l: temple of Venus at Eryx, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The temple of Venus at Eryx stood on the summit of a high and craggy hill and was richly furnished and adorned with offerings. Daedalus enlarged and fortified the site by building a wall around the summit and making the area level and spacious.

l: Minos's invasion of Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_caused_by Daedalus [Minos sought to punish him] Minos's invasion of Sicily began after he learned that Daedalus had fled there. Minos sailed with a great fleet to the coast of Agrigentum, demanded Daedalus from Cocalus, and was killed during the ensuing encounter.

l: Minos's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_caused_by Cocalus [through suffocation in a hot bath] Minos's death occurred when Cocalus kept him in a hot bath until the steam and heat suffocated him. The Cretans buried him with great ceremony in a double sepulchre and established a temple to Venus near the visible upper part.

l: temple of the Curetes or Corybantes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_dedicated_to Curetes [in Sicily] The temple of the Curetes or Corybantes was built by Cretans who had settled in Sicily and was richly adorned with gifts. Its stones were brought from the Agyrians over a rough route a hundred furlongs long, and the temple possessed extensive lands and large sacred treasures.

l: Cyrene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_daughter_of Hypsaeus Cyrene was the beautiful daughter of Hypsaeus and the mother of Aristaeus by Apollo. Apollo carried her to Libya, where a city named Cyrene was later founded after her.

l: plague at Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The plague at Athens was accompanied by famine and was attributed in the account to wet weather, stagnant and polluted water, spoiled food, and the absence of the usual Etesian winds. Many Athenians suffered burning illnesses, and the city lost large numbers of soldiers, cavalry, servants, and others.

l: Berei Mountains, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a mountain range [in Sicily, pleasant and fertile] The Berei Mountains in Sicily were described as a pleasant region with sweet air, abundant springs, groves of lime and oak, edible roots and bulbs, and many melons. They contained a beautiful valley and a grove dedicated to the nymphs, where Daphnis was said to have been born.

l: Orion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Orion is the biggest and strongest of all heroes, much given to hunting. Seeking vain glory, he performs great actions: he builds Acte for Zanclus, raises Pelorus in the open sea, and builds a temple to Neptune there. He then sails to and resides in Euboea, and is represented by Orion constellation among the stars for his actions.

l: Messana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Messana is a city, anciently called Zancle and afterwards Messana; its earlier name was linked to Zanclus and the harbour Acte. Himilco captured it after a Carthaginian fleet entered its harbour, with inhabitants killed, captured, or driven away, then demolished it almost completely. Dionysius later fortified it, and its townsmen and his mercenaries defeated Heloris amid further campaigning.

l: Euboea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Euboea is an island containing Artemisium, where the Grecian fleet assembled and was stationed against the enemy; it joined the Greek confederacy against Sparta, then suffered Persian capture of Istiaea, devastation, and destruction.

l: Orion constellation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Orion, named after Orion, was fixed among the stars as a constellation in recognition of the glory of his actions, making his name famous for eternity.

l: Book V, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a historical book Book V begins with Sicily and proceeds to the Aeolian Islands, Lipara, and Osteodes. It discusses geography, origins, religious traditions, peoples, colonization, volcanic activity, and notable events.

l: Trinacria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Trinacria, principal city of the Siculi, was wealthy, independent of Syracusan control, and noted for many valiant men and brave commanders; lacking assistance, it was defeated by Syracuse, its inhabitants enslaved, and the city razed.

l: Sicanians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Sicanians, described as Sicily’s first inhabitants, lived in villages and fortified hill towns under separate princes. Accounts dispute whether they came from Iberia or were indigenous; volcanic destruction drove them westward, where conflict with the Sicilians ended in established boundaries.

l: Sicilians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Sicilians are a people said to have moved from Italy into Sicily with their families after the Sicanians withdrew from parts of the island. They spread into neighboring lands, fought the Sicanians, and gave the island its name. Once frightened by barbarian forces, they regained courage after Gelon’s victory and honored his modest and humane rule. Under Dionysius, they first supported him, but hatred led many to side with the Carthaginians, defend Messana, or retreat to forts. After the Carthaginian rout, those allies escaped to their cities. At Taurominium, they resisted Dionysius, expelled his forces, and killed more than six hundred men.

l: Enna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_located_in Sicily [near the center of the island] Enna is described as lying near a fragrant meadow filled with violets and other flowers. The meadow is presented as the place where Proserpine was carried away, with a cave and underground passage associated with Pluto’s departure.

l: Himera, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Himera is a Sicilian Greek city defended by Theron and later threatened by Carthaginian armies. After Amilcar's siege, Gelon's arrival helps defeat and drive off the attackers, making it a site of a Greek victory over Carthage. Its people later plot with Hiero against Theron, are punished, and receive Dorian settlers. After Selinus's destruction, Hannibal besieges, captures, plunders, burns, and razes Himera.

l: Mount Etna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Mount Etna is described as a source of fire and as a place whose eruptions damaged and laid waste to Sicilian territory. Ceres is said to have lit her firebrands at its eruptions while searching for Proserpine. Etna, formerly called Eunetia, became the refuge of the Cataneans after they were forced to leave Catana.

l: Strongyle, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Strongyle, formerly called Dia, was Naxus: Thracian settlers, including Butes, practiced piracy and held it over two hundred years until drought and famine drove them away.

l: Leontium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
